content: Did the linter accidentally get turned off?
Do I understand the linter code correctly that this is potentially reparsing the entire current file for every single command in it?
It does reparse the whole file, but only for commands up to the first module doc. (This is the effect up to the unless stx.getTailPos?.getD default ≤ firstDocModPos do return line.)
And if there is no module doc?

Then it only calls parseHeader:

  -- We try to parse the file up to `firstDocModPos`.
  let upToStx ← parseUpToHere firstDocModPos <|> (do
    -- If parsing failed, there is some command which is not a module docstring.
    -- In that case, we parse until the end of the imports and add an extra `section` afterwards,
    -- so we trigger a "no module doc-string" warning.
    let fil ← getFileName
    let (stx, _) ← Parser.parseHeader { inputString := fm.source, fileName := fil, fileMap := fm }
    parseUpToHere (stx.raw.getTailPos?.getD default) "\nsection")

Please take another look at th definition of firstMDDocModPos

The end of the first module doc-string, or the end of the file if there is none

All that the linter needs to know is what the first command after the imports is. The intention is also that, once the linter is active, any compliant file will have a module doc and the test will be quick.
However, if there is a way of getting the kind of the first non-import command of a file, I would be really happy to know!

Sebastian Ullrich said:

Do I understand the linter code correctly that this is potentially reparsing the entire current file for every single command in it?

Yes, and the number and location of error messages this produces for a failing file is mildly confusing in my experience of fixing these errors for CSLib. Since this was included in mathlibStandardSet but silently not running outside Mathlib, I might expect some confusion downstream on updating.

Damiano Testa said:

However, if there is a way of getting the kind of the first non-import command of a file, I would be really happy to know!

I think we would first have to determine what the appropriate scope and trigger for a linter of this kind should be. In its current implementation, having this as a syntax linter is fundamentally broken as it looks at downstream inputs (Mathlib.lean) such that it can get you into situations where the result of lake build is not deterministic!

With respect to parsing the whole file, what do you think of using

import Lean.Parser.Extension

open Lean Elab Parser in
def captureException (env : Environment) (s : ParserFn) (input : String) : Option Syntax :=
  let ictx := mkInputContext input "<input>"
  let s := s.run ictx { env, options := {} } (getTokenTable env) (mkParserState input)
  dbg_trace s.stxStack.back
  if !s.allErrors.isEmpty then
    none
  else
    s.stxStack.back

instead?

Modulo figuring out whether there are comments/whitespace or not start from the parseImports stops, if captureException is successful and the resulting syntax is of kind moduleDoc, then it passes the check, otherwise the first command is not a module doc, but you do not have to parse the whole file.
@Damiano Testa That sounds roughly correct for that specific part
This should at least reduce build times, although I understand that it does not address the "read Mathlib.lean" issue.
Wouldn't this only speed up the "no (misplaced) module docs" worst case that shouldn't happen in Mathlib? Likely some actual performance profiling would need to be done to identify the bottlenecks

Yes, if a file is compliant with the linter, I think that the above is probably very similar performance-wise to the current version. However, if a downstream project has the linter on because it comes from mathlibLinterSet, then there it could affect performance much more.
Ok, I thought you were talking specifically about the perf diff we saw from the linter apparently(?) being deactivated in Mathlib
In any case, parsing whatever comes after the imports to figure out if there is a doc-string seems like a much simpler and direct algorithm than the one currently used by the linter.

Sebastian Ullrich said:

Ok, I thought you were talking specifically about the perf diff we saw from the linter apparently(?) being deactivated in Mathlib

For this, I agree that it would require some profiling. I wonder if, in the end, it is the string parsing that was written before the change in the string API changes and when I had even less of a clue about how to work with strings than now.

Well, I assume one major part is that this limited parsing would still be done once per command in the file, no? I assume the proper solution would be to rely purely on the info tree here and use it to immediately tell whether we are more than one command into the file. I believe linters do not currently have access to the info trees above the current command and there were prior discussions about that but did they ever culminate into an RFC?
21 messages were moved here from #rss > Significant commits to mathlib4 by Sebastian Ullrich.
As far as I know, linters only have access to the infotrees of the current command. I also do not think that there is an RFC for this.
You could avoid the parsing sometimes, by checking first if the file contains a declaration already, inspecting the declarationRanges extension. I do not know if this would be quicker.
(It also does not help with files that do not add declarations, though those are probably rare.)
